title: Measurement-based uncomputation of quantum circuits for modular arithmetic
problem: Quantum circuits for modular arithmetic suffer from high Toffoli gate counts and circuit depths, limiting their applicability in resource-constrained quantum systems.
motivation: Reducing quantum circuit complexity (gate count, depth) is critical for near-term quantum computing applications, particularly in cryptanalysis where modular arithmetic is fundamental.
method: This approach uses measurement-based uncomputation (MBU)—a technique where quantum measurement results eliminate the need for certain quantum gates—applied to single-qubit registers performing modular arithmetic. Rather than building all gates upfront, MBU probabilistically uses measurement outcomes to skip expensive Toffoli gates (the most resource-intensive operations in quantum circuits). The method is formalized specifically for modular arithmetic and tested across different modular adder architectures to verify it reduces both Toffoli gate counts and circuit depth.
key_novelty: The core contribution is formalizing measurement-based uncomputation for single-qubit modular arithmetic circuits, showing how quantum measurement outcomes can reduce Toffoli gate counts and circuit depth in resource-constrained quantum systems.
contributions: 10-15% reduction in Toffoli count for MBU-based modular adders
Nearly 25% reduction for adders in alternative architectures
Potential extension to modular multiplication and exponentiation
Applications to quantum cryptanalysis of RSA-like systems
limitations: Limited to single-qubit registers; applicability to larger quantum systems and practical quantum processors not discussed.
primary_theme: quantum circuit optimization via measurement-based uncomputation
